q1: SELECT b1.name AS bar1, b2.name AS bar2 FROM bar AS b1, bar AS b2 WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT s1.beer FROM serves AS s1 WHERE s1.bar = b1.name AND NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM serves AS s2 WHERE s2.bar = b2.name AND s2.beer = s1.beer)) AND EXISTS(SELECT s2.beer FROM serves AS s2 WHERE s2.bar = b2.name AND NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM serves AS s1 WHERE s1.bar = b1.name AND s1.beer = s2.beer))
q2: SELECT DISTINCT serves1.bar, serves2.bar FROM serves AS serves1 RIGHT OUTER JOIN serves AS serves2 ON serves1.beer = serves2.beer AND serves1.bar <> serves2.bar

counterexample: INSERT INTO Bar (name, address) VALUES ('BarA', 'AddressA'), ('BarB', 'AddressB'); INSERT INTO Beer (name, brewer) VALUES ('X', 'BrewerX'), ('Y', 'BrewerY'); INSERT INTO Serves (bar, beer, price) VALUES ('BarA', 'X', 10.00), ('BarA', 'Y', 12.00), ('BarB', 'X', 11.00);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent. Q1 checks for bars that serve all beers served by another bar and at least one beer that no other bar serves. Q2, on the other hand, uses a right outer join to find pairs of bars that serve the same beer but are different.
counterexample_dsp: Create two bars, BarA and BarB, where BarA serves beer X and beer Y, and BarB serves beer X. This setup triggers the difference as Q1 will not find a match for BarA, while Q2 will find a match for the pair (BarA, BarB).
